paper_title: PolyRoute: A Twelve-Language and Code-Mixed Benchmark for Typed-Decision Routing, with Baselines and a Leaderboard

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.

sections.title: Key	findings
sections.content: 1. Dataset. 322 native items (12 languages, 5 script groups) and 156 code-mixed items; independent-labeller agreement 97.2% [94.898.5], lowest in Spanish (86%); no test text has 5-gram Jaccard similarity above 0.33 to any training text. 2. Tracks separate, the top does not. Shipped checkpoints 61%/63%/77%; fine-tuned multilingual systems 94%97%; 4 systems are statistically tied with the best entry. 3. Strong cheap baselines. TF-IDF + logistic regression on all rows scores 91.9%; an independent LLM scores 97.2%. 4. Weak spots are script groups, not token counts. Fertilityaccuracy correlation ρ=-0.34 (root) and -0.17 (shipped multilingual), n=12; the shipped checkpoint is weakest on the Indic group (63%). 5. Reduced-exposure transfer. On four withheld languages: shipped 77%, no per-language rows 91%, withheldlanguage fine-tune 90%, all-language fine-tune 93%; the base rows already contain about 30 generic rows per language. 6. Code-mixed text is different test. The English-root fine-tune scores 96% on code-mixed items but 74% on native text; the English root is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (85% vs 79%, p=0.134). 7. Resolution limit and pitfalls. Differences below about 4 points among the top systems are unresolvable at n=322; rotating option names drops the best fine-tune to 7%.

sections.title: 1		Motivation	and	contributions
sections.content: A typed-decision encoder answers question about piece of text in one forward pass: it reads one hidden state per answer option and returns distribution over the options, with no token-by-token generation. For support desk that is attractive, because routing becomes cheap and predictable. What deployment cannot take for granted is that such an encoder behaves in other languages as it does in the one it was developed in. The public model family we study ships an English ModernBERT-large root [Warner et al. 2024] (421M parameters) and separate multilingual checkpoint (322M parameters, 256k-token vocabulary), with small router that chooses between them. Which checkpoint to trust for which language, and how much task-specific fine-tuning adds, are questions that need fixed yardstick, not ad-hoc spot checks. This paper provides one. PolyRoute is test collection of 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, second collection of 156 code-mixed and romanised messages, an optional pool of 967 native training rows, and an evaluation protocol with documented baselines. The question is deliberately simple (three departments), so that the quantity under test is the language and not the difficulty of the question. The format is the typed decision used by the model family, which lets every item be scored for accuracy, calibration and selective prediction with no prompt engineering. Intended uses. (i) Comparing multilingual encoders or fine-tuning recipes on routing-style decisions; (ii) auditing system for language gaps before deployment; (iii) studying cross-lingual transfer through ready-made withheld-language variant; (iv) testing robustness to code-mixed text. Not intended as measurement of real-world traffic: all texts are LLMwritten (Section 13).

sections.title: 1.1		Contributions
sections.content: 1. native-language test split with per-language label statistics and an independent label audit (97.2% agreement; lowest in Spanish at 86%). 2. code-mixed split (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi) disjoint from every training file. 3. Five fine-tuning sets with nested native content, one of them withholding four languages, together with an explicit account of what each contains including block of 399 generic multilingual rows that even the withheld set still contains. 4. leaderboard of 13 systems with intervals, rank-stability analysis and the smallest difference the split can resolve ( of 78 system pairs are separated at p<0.01). 5. Analyses user will want to reproduce: per language and script, tokenizer fertility, the shipped router, learning curve, transfer to withheld languages, calibration, stress conditions and an error taxonomy with real examples.

sections.title: 1.2		Where	it	sits	among	multilingual	benchmarks
sections.content: Established suites such as XNLI [Conneau et al. 2018] and XTREME [Hu et al. 2020] test cross-lingual transfer on standard tasks, built on multilingual pre-trained encoders [Pires et al. 2019; Conneau et al. 2020]; English intent-detection sets such as Banking77 [Casanueva et al. 2020] are the closest in task shape; MASSIVE [FitzGerald et al. 2022] covers intent classification in 51 languages with human translation; GLUECoS [Khanuja et al. 2020] targets code-switching. PolyRoute is narrower. It fixes one decision type and one question text and is shaped by the typed-decision interface, so that models which score options through placeholder tokens can be evaluated without generation step. The price of that narrowness is that conclusions about other tasks do not follow; the benefit is compact split with documented provenance. We follow datasheet [Gebru et al. 2018] and data-statement [Bender and Friedman 2018] practice in Sections 4 and 13, and the advice on statistical power in NLP evaluation [Card et al. 2020; Berg-Kirkpatrick et al. 2012] in Section 7. Table 1. The benchmark at glance. sections.title: 2.1		The	typed	decision
sections.content: Every item is pair (text, question). The question is of type choice: an instruction (Which department should handle this?) and an ordered set of named options with one-line description each: billing (invoices, payments, refunds), technical (bugs, outages, system errors) and other (everything else). Instruction and options are in English in every item whatever the language of the message, mirroring deployment in which the operator writes the schema once and messages arrive in many languages. The gold answer is one option.

sections.title: 2.2		How	the	model	under	test	reads	an	item
sections.content: The Laya family packs question and text into one sequence: classification token, the question and instruction, separator, placeholder token in front of each option name and description, separator, and the message, truncated to 512 tokens in total (192 for the question part). The encoder runs once; two-layer option head reads the hidden state at each placeholder and emits one score per option, and softmax over the scores gives the confidence. The root checkpoint has 28 encoder layers of width 1024; the multilingual checkpoint has 22 layers of width 768, with 61% of its parameters in the embedding table. Neither the data nor the metrics depend on this architecture: any system that returns distribution over the three options can be submitted. Figure 1. The benchmark item. message and typed question are packed into one sequence with placeholder in front of each option; the model reads the hidden state at every placeholder and returns one probability per option (the numbers shown are the actual output of the best fine-tuned system on the first test item).

sections.title: 2.3		Why	routing
sections.content: Department routing is topical: the cue is lexical or semantic (a refund, an outage) and not syntactic (negation, word order). That keeps the items answerable in every language with simple vocabulary, so an error is unlikely to be explained by the question being too hard for native speaker. The price is high ceiling: tuned systems score above 95% (Section 8), so the benchmark discriminates mainly among systems not tuned to it, and Section 7 quantifies how little room is left at the top.

sections.title: 3.1		Generation
sections.content: For each language and each department the teacher model (Qwen3.8-27B, sampling temperature 0.9) is asked for up to ten diverse, realistic support messages in that language only, in its native script, with no English words except product names, each of which has the requested department as its correct answer (label-conditioned self-generation in the style of [Wang et al. 2022]); length, style and vocabulary are varied through per-call variation seed. Across the native test split and the native training rows this produced 1,420 candidate texts.

sections.title: 3.2		Blind	filtering
sections.content: The candidates of each call are shown to the same model again without their intended labels, together with the three options, and it picks one option per text. text survives only if the blind choice equals the intended label: 1,289 of 1,420 candidates (90.8%) did. Retention differs by department (billing 95%, technical 97%, other 80%) and by language, from 86% for Hindi to 97% for Turkish (Figure 2). The filter removes some genuinely ambiguous messages, but it is selfconsistency check and not human one, which is why Section 5 adds an audit by different model family. Figure 2. Filter retention for every language-by-label cell. Low cells flag where the teachers intended label and its blind reading diverge, which is first, language-level indicator of label difficulty.

sections.title: 3.3		Separation	of	files
sections.content: The test split (322 items) and the training rows (967 rows) come from two generation runs with different variation seeds, and during each run any text identical to text in another split file is dropped. The code-mixed split was generated the same way from three prompts: Hindi in Latin letters freely mixed with English; Spanish mixed with English inside sentence; and Arabic written in Latin letters and digits, mixed with English. The prompts ask for chat-like text and not for textbook code-switching. Of 180 candidates, 158 passed the filter and 156 are in the released file. Figure 3. How the benchmark files were produced and what survived at each step (counts are the real generation log; the test split and the native training rows come from separate generation runs with different variation seeds).

sections.title: 4.1		Length	and	tokenization
sections.content: Character length varies by factor of 4.6 between languages (the shortest messages, in characters, are Korean, Chinese, Japanese), but token counts matter more to an encoder. The English-root tokenizer needs 2.0 as many tokens as the multilingual one on average, and up to 3.1 for Tamil  (Table 2)  . The longest message is 211 root tokens, so truncation at 512 tokens never occurs: inflation changes what the model sees, not how much of it.

sections.title: 4.3		A	block	of	generic	multilingual	rows	in	the	base	training	set
sections.content: The 2,818 base fine-tuning rows, shared by every training track, include 399 department-routing rows produced by an earlier generic prompt that asked for texts in different language from list of twelve. They are not labelled by language; by dominant script they split as Latin 138, Han + kana 34, Arabic 34, Cyrillic 33, Han 33, Bengali 33, Hangul 32, Tamil 31, Devanagari 31, i.e. roughly 3035 rows for each non-Latin language. They are disjoint from the test split by the filters of Section 3, but they mean that no training track is free of exposure to the twelve languages. The track names below say no per-language rows or withheld, never zero-shot.

sections.title: 4.4		Language	fidelity	of	the	generated	text
sections.content: The script-purity column of Table 2 is coarse check. Two cheap, stricter checks find generation artefacts that we left in place. First, 3 of the 217 non-Latin-script test messages contain at least one letter from writing system that is neither the expected one nor Latin (Bengali 1, Hindi 1, Japanese 1). Second, stop-word heuristic flags 2 of the 105 Latin-script test messages as English text filed under Turkish, which script purity cannot detect. These items are valid routing questions with correct departments, but they are not clean samples of the named language, and user who needs strictly monolingual text should filter them (the indices are reproducible from the released file).

sections.title: 5.1		Independent	labelling
sections.content: Because the gold labels come from one model family, we asked different family (gemma4-31b) to label every test item blind, with the same prompt format as the generation-time filter. It agrees with the gold label on 313 of 322 items (97.2% [94.898.5]). Agreement is high in every language (Figure 4): the lowest per-language point estimate is Spanish (86%, 4 of 28 items disputed) and 6 of 12 languages are at 100%. At about 27 items per language the intervals are wide, and only Spanish is distinguishable from the pooled value by eye; we make no per-language claims about label quality. Figure 4. Label quality measured by an independent model family. Left: per-language agreement of gemma4-31b with the gold label (band: interval for the pooled split; dashed line: pooled agreement). Right: gold-versus-independent confusion counts; the off-diagonal cells are the disputed items. The disagreements are not spread evenly across departments: agreement is 99.2% for billing (n=118), 99.1% for technical (n=116), 92.0% for other (n=88). The most frequent cell is gold other labelled technical by the independent model (6 items), consistent with the residual class being the least well delimited: message that mentions payment problem caused by an outage can legitimately be argued either way. We define the consensus subset as the 313 items on which both labellers agree, and report it as secondary view in the leaderboard (the confusion counts are in the right panel of Figure 4).

sections.title: 5.2		Does	label	noise	explain	the	model	errors?
sections.content: It can be bounded directly. The best fine-tuned system (ML fine-tune, all native rows) scores 97.1% on the consensus subset against 77.8% on the 9 disputed items; the shipped multilingual checkpoint scores 79.2% against 11.1%. Systems are less accurate on disputed items, as expected when gold labels are noisy there, but the 9 disputed items could account for at most 9 of the 125 errors of the root checkpoint, so the gap between weak and strong systems is real and not an artefact of the labels. For strong systems the picture is different: 2 of the 11 errors of the best fine-tuned system fall on disputed items (a minority), so label noise is visible but not dominant share of what remains.

sections.title: 5.3		Leakage	audit
sections.content: For every test text we computed the maximum Jaccard similarity of its character 5-gram set to any text in the pool of all 3,785 training rows (and, for the native split, to the rest of the test split). Table 4 and Figure 5 summarise the result: no native test text exceeds 0.33 against the training pool, no code-mixed text exceeds 0.20, and the most similar pair of native test texts has similarity 0.17; there are 0 exact duplicates with training rows and 0 inside the test split. Several items in the same language share topical vocabulary (refund, invoice, crash), which probably accounts for most of the similarity mass near 0.050.15, but nothing resembling character-level near-duplicate (a paraphrase would not be caught by this measure). sections.title: 6.3		Evaluation	protocol
sections.content: 1. Present each item with the fixed question text and the options in the canonical order (billing, technical, other); do not rename options, because Section 10 shows how strongly the models follow option names. 2. Obtain one probability per option; the prediction is the arg-max, the confidence is its probability. 3. Report accuracy with Wilson interval on the native split and, separately, on the code-mixed split; also report language-macro accuracy and the worst language. 4. For pairwise claims use an exact McNemar test on the shared items and state the number of comparisons made. 5. Never tune on the test items; if threshold is calibrated, calibrate it on held-out part of the training rows. 6. Declare the exposure of the fine-tuning set to the twelve languages (including generic multilingual rows) and the number of seeds.

sections.title: 7.2		How	large	a	difference	can	the	split	resolve?
sections.content: A benchmark with 322 items cannot rank systems whose accuracies are close. For paired comparison in which two systems disagree on fraction of the items, the smallest difference detectable at α=0.01 with 80% power is about 3.42(d/n) (a normal approximation to McNemars test). Table 8 evaluates this for the sizes that occur in this benchmark; Figure 7 shows the curve and places every pair of leaderboard systems against it. The top five fine-tuned systems disagree on 3.6% of the items on average, so on the native split the resolvable difference among them is 3.6 points larger than the largest gap between them (2.8 points). For single language (about 26 items) even 25%-discordant pair needs 34point gap, which is why we do not rank systems per language. We use the single threshold p<0.01 without correction for the 78 leaderboard pairs; with Bonferroni threshold of 0.01/78, 48 of the 55 separated pairs remain separated. Anyone claiming gain of few points should repeat training with several seeds and use the paired bootstrap over items. Table 8. sections.title: 8.2		Leaderboard
sections.content: Tables 10 and 11 give the full results; Figure 8 draws the primary metric. Four observations follow. 1. Tracks separate cleanly; the top does not. The shipped checkpoints (track A) score 61.2%, 62.7% and 77.3%; every fine-tuned multilingual system (tracks and C) scores between 93.8% and 96.6%. The highest accuracy is gemma4-31b as classifier at 97.2%, and 4 other systems cannot be separated from it at p<0.01 (ML FT w/o 4 langs, ML FT 25%, ML FT 50%, ML FT 100%). Params ms / item 421M 1.6 1. 1.2 3.1 2.1 / 2. networkbound as root as shipped as shipped as shipped as shipped 2. bag of n-grams is serious baseline. TF-IDF + LR trained on all rows scores 91.9%, +4.7 points (p=0.014) from the best fine-tuned model; trained on the base rows only it scores 77.0%, level with the shipped multilingual checkpoint (-0.3 points (p=1.000) for TF-IDF relative to it). Department routing is lexically easy, and any claim about multilingual encoder on this task has to be read against that. 3. An independent LLM, used as classifier, is strong reference. gemma4-31b agrees with the gold labels on 97.2%, +0.6 points (p=0.804) relative to the best fine-tuned model. It was not trained on these labels, so this is also ceiling of sorts for the label audit; it costs hosted model and network round trip per item, against 2.0 ms for the fine-tuned encoder. 4. Multilingual fine-tunes are better calibrated. ECE falls from 0.058 (root) and 0.078 (shipped multilingual) to 0.011 for the best fine-tune, whereas the English-root fine-tune has 0.166 (Section 10). Table 10. Leaderboard, part 1: accuracy and probabilistic quality on the 322-item native split. sections.content: Resampling the test items 2,000 times (Figure 9) shows how well each position is determined. sections.title: 8.4		Seed	variation
sections.content: Three seeds of the best recipe score 96.6%, 96.9%, 95.7% (standard deviation 0.6 points, range 1.2). Any two seeds answer 2.7% of the items differently, floor on the discordance that one-seed comparison cannot get below. For comparison, the 25%, 50% and 100% native-row models differ from one another by 1.9 points; that exceeds the seed-toseed range, but it is small against the sampling interval, so we treat them as one cluster in the rest of the paper.

sections.title: 9.3		Tokenizer	fertility	and	resource	tier
sections.content: Tokenizer fragmentation is the usual explanation for weak performance on non-Latin scripts [Rust et al. 2021; Ahia et al. 2023; Petrov et al. 2023]. We test it on the benchmark with the standard fertility measure (tokens per character). Across the twelve languages the Spearman correlation between fertility and accuracy is ρ=-0.34 for the root checkpoint with its own tokenizer (permutation p=0.28) and ρ=-0.17 for the shipped multilingual one (p=0.60): moderate negative and negligible negative respectively, and neither is distinguishable from zero at n=12. The ratio of root to multilingual token counts per language correlates with the accuracy gain from root to multilingual at ρ=+0.47. Figure 11 shows why correlations are weak: the three highest-fertility languages under the root tokenizer are Korean (62%), Chinese (79%), Tamil (36%) and the three lowest are Spanish (68%), Portuguese (82%), German (81%), so accuracy does not follow fragmentation monotonically. moderate negative correlation is compatible with these data and cannot be excluded at n=12, but fertility alone is not usable predictor of per-language accuracy on this task; it is also compatible with accounts in which the amount of pre-training data per language matters [Wu and Dredze 2020]. Figure 11. Accuracy against tokenizer fertility for each language, coloured by the coarse resource tier used in this paper (an author-assigned grouping, not measurement). Grouping the languages by coarse resource tier (high: German, Portuguese, Spanish, Russian, Chinese, Japanese; mid: Turkish, Arabic, Hindi, Korean; low: Bengali, Tamil; an author-assigned grouping in the spirit of [Joshi et al. 2020], not measurement) gives Table 13. sections.title: 12		Recommended	usage	and	pitfalls
sections.content: Report the two splits separately. The English-root fine-tune and the shipped multilingual checkpoint score 73.6% and 77.3% on the native split (3.7 points apart) but 96.2% and 79.5% on the code-mixed split (16.7 points apart). single pooled number would hide that the two splits measure different things. Do not rank systems within about 4 points of each other on the native split. The split cannot resolve it (Section 7); use several seeds (0.6 points of seed standard deviation here) and the paired bootstrap. Do not make per-language claims from this split. About 26 items per language give cell intervals of roughly 11 19 points. Pool by script group or tier if language-level statement is needed. Keep the question text and option names fixed. Rotating the names while keeping the descriptions reduces the best fine-tune to 6.5%  (Table 18)  ; changing the schema changes the task. Read the withheld-language track as reduced exposure. The base rows hold 399 generic multilingual texts (Section 4.3). Compare with bag of n-grams. TF-IDF + LR on all rows reaches 91.9%; multilingual-encoder result is informative only to the extent that it exceeds what lexical cues give. Use the consensus subset as sanity check, not as the headline. It removes 9 disputed items and changes the best systems accuracy from 96.6% to 97.1%. Do not tune on the test items. Both splits are small enough to be over-fitted by repeated model selection [Bowman and Dahl 2021].

sections.title: 13		Limitations,	ethics	and	datasheet
sections.content: Table 23 condenses the datasheet; the paragraphs below spell out the limitations that bear most on how the benchmark should be used. Table 23. Datasheet (condensed). Section Question Answer Motivation Why was it created? To give typed-decision encoders fixed, documented multilingual routing test, with baselines, instead of ad-hoc spot checks. Motivation Who created it? The authors, as part of an evaluation of public typed-decision model family; no external dataset was used. Composition What are the instances? short support message in one of 12 languages (or code-mixed) with one gold department out of three. Test: 322 native + 156 code-mixed; optional training: 967 native rows. Composition Is there personal or sensitive data? No. All texts are generated by language model from topical prompt; no real users, names or accounts are involved, although generated texts may contain invented names and amounts. Composition Are labels reliable? They are LLM-made and self-consistency filtered; an independent model family agrees on 97.2%. No human annotation was done. Collection How was it collected? Teacher-model generation per language and department, blind relabelling by the same model, exact-text de-duplication against other splits (Section 3). Preprocessing Was anything removed? Candidates whose blind label disagreed with the intended label (131 of 1420 native-run candidates, 22 of 180 code-mixed candidates). No other cleaning; messages are used verbatim. Uses Uses Recommended uses Uses to avoid Model comparison on routing-style decisions across languages; transfer and robustness studies; calibration studies. Estimating real-world performance in language; ranking languages; training production systems without additional human-written data; any claim about speaker community. Distribution Where are the files and how to verify them? In the projects data directory as JSON-lines; SHA-256 checksums are in Appendix C. Check the terms of the teacher model before redistributing generated text. Maintenance Will it be updated? The files are frozen with the results; human-written replacement for at least the test split is the intended next version.

sections.title: 13.1		Limitations
sections.content: All labels and texts are LLM-made. The labels were produced and filtered by one model family; the independent audit (97.2%) bounds but does not remove the dependence, and agreement between two language models is not agreement with speakers [Northcutt et al. 2021; Zheng et al. 2023]. The text itself may be more regular and more standard than what customers write; dialect, typos, scripts mixed within word and domain vocabulary are underrepresented. Machine-written text in low-resource languages. The teachers fluency and cultural fit probably vary across the twelve languages; no native speaker has reviewed the texts. This matters most for Tamil and Bengali. One task, one schema. Routing is topical and has high ceiling (97.2% for the best entry); the benchmark says little about tasks where syntax or negation decides. Small cells. About 26 items per language and 156 code-mixed items: only large gaps are resolvable (Section 7). Exposure in the base rows. 399 generic multilingual rows are shared by all training tracks. Other limits. Generated text contains artefacts (foreign-script fragments, English text filed under Latin-script language; Section 4.4); only the best recipe has three seeds (the others are single runs); the resource tiers are an authorassigned grouping, not measurement; and no classical or LLM baseline was run on the code-mixed split.

sections.title: 13.2		Ethical	considerations
sections.content: The data contain no real personal information. The main risk is over-reading: benchmark of synthetic text could be used to certify system for lower-resource-language speakers who were never represented in it, and router that is wrong more often for some languages would then deliver slower or wrong service to those users. We therefore ask that results be reported with the intervals, the split names and the withheld-language caveat above, and that deployments be validated on human-written messages from the target community. Generated text can also carry the teachers stereotypes about languages and countries; we did not audit for that. Compute cost is small: the benchmark runs in seconds on one GPU (2.0 ms per item for the best encoder).

sections.title: 14		Conclusion
sections.content: PolyRoute turns the question does this typed-decision encoder work outside English? into measurement with documented provenance: 322 native-language messages in 12 languages, 156 code-mixed ones, an independent label audit (97.2% agreement), leakage audit (maximum similarity 0.33), five nested training sets and thirteen leaderboard entries. The first results are that the English root scores 61.2% and the shipped multilingual checkpoint 77.3%; fine-tuning the multilingual encoder reaches 96.6% and most of that gain needs no dedicated native rows; bag of n-grams is within 5 points of the best fine-tune; and on code-mixed text the English root is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (85% vs 79%, p=0.134). The split cannot separate systems closer than about 4 points, and its labels, texts and languages come from language models; those limits, not the leaderboard, are the main message for anyone who builds on it.

sections.title: Appendix	D		Prompts	and	scoring	recipe
sections.content: D.1 Generation request (paraphrased) Write (at most 10) diverse, realistic inputs for classifier. Question: Which department should handle this? The correct answer for every input must be <department> (with its one-line description). Write every text in <language> only (native script), with no English words except product names. Make them unambiguous to careful human and vary length, style and vocabulary (variation seed s). Return only JSON array of strings. D.2 Blind relabelling request (paraphrased) Question and the three options with their descriptions are shown, followed by the numbered texts of one call; for each text choose exactly one option key; return only JSON array of keys in order. The intended label is not shown. text is kept if and only if the returned key equals the intended label. D.3 Scoring recipe 1. Load data/ml_test.jsonl and data/mix_test.jsonl; each row has state (the message), questions (the typed question) and expected (the gold option). 2. For every row build the input exactly as published and obtain one probability per option in the order billing, technical, other. 3. Prediction = arg-max; confidence = its probability; correct = prediction equals the gold option. 4. Report accuracy with Wilson interval, language-macro accuracy, worst language, macro-F1, NLL and ECE, on the native and code-mixed splits separately, and the track under which the system was trained.
